In mathematics, especially [[category theory]], '''limits''' and '''colimits''' in an [[∞-category]] generalize [[limit (category theory)|limit]]s and [[colimit (category theory)|colimit]]s in a category. Like the counterparts in ordinary category theory, they play fundamental roles in constructions (e.g., [[Kan extension]]s) as well as characterizations (e.g., sheaf conditions) in [[higher category theory]].

== Definition ==
Let <math>I</math> be a simplicial set and <math>C</math> an ∞-category (a weak Kan complex). Fix a [[Grothendieck universe]]. Then, roughly, a limit of a functor <math>f : I \to C</math> amounts to the following isomorphism:
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(a_{\textrm{const}}, f) \overset{\sim}\to \operatorname{Hom}(a, \varprojlim f)</math>
functorially in <math>a</math>,<ref>{{harvnb|Cisinski|2023|loc=Remark 6.2.5.}}</ref> where <math>a_{\textrm{const}} : I \to C</math> denotes the constant functor with value <math>a</math>.

A typical case is when <math>I = \Delta</math> is the simplex category or rather its opposite; in the latter case, the functor <math>f</math> is commonly called a [[simplicial diagram]].

== Facts ==
The ordinary category of sets has small limits and colimits. Similarly,
*The ∞-category of ∞-categories and the ∞-category of Kan complexes both have all small limits and colimits.<ref>{{harvnb|Land|2021|loc=Theorem 4.3.37.}}</ref>
*The presheaf category <math>\mathcal{P}(C) = \textbf{Fct}(C, \textbf{Kan})</math> on an ∞-category ''C'' has colimits, as a consequence of the above.<ref>{{harvnb|Cisinski|2023|loc=Proposition 6.2.12.}}</ref>

Also, many of standard facts about limits and colimits in a category continue to hold for those in an ∞-category.
*An ∞-category has all small limits if and only if it has coequalizers and small coproducts.<ref>{{harvnb|Lurie|2009|loc=Proposition 4.4.3.2.}}</ref>
*If a functor admits a left adjoint, then it commutes with all limits.<ref>{{harvnb|Cisinski|2023|loc=Proposition 6.2.15.}}</ref>
